active_themes.label: Warsh Chair Confirmed
active_themes.summary: Kevin Warsh takes office this week. Powell's exit is ceremonial. The market's working assumption—that Warsh prioritizes financial conditions over inflation and will cut rates—is now locked in. The open question shifts: not whether cuts happen, but whether cuts arriving into $90+ oil, weak dollar fundamentals, and tightening consumer credit will trigger a second inflation wave that forces reversal before full effect.

active_themes.label: Oil Holds $90+ Floor
active_themes.summary: Trump delayed Iran strikes today. Oil initially fell over 1% before recovering to close unchanged at $91. The reprieve is temporary. Oil's refusal to fall hard on dovish news signals that $90+ is now priced into supply-demand structure, not just geopolitical headlines. With Warsh confirmed and the dollar primed to weaken into rate cuts, the market expects oil to hold or move higher regardless of Iran developments.

active_themes.label: Lenders Front-Running Cuts
active_themes.summary: Warsh's confirmation removed the last uncertainty around Fed policy direction. Rational lenders now have the clearest possible signal to withdraw credit before the competitive race for lower-yield lending intensifies. No major lender announcement today, but the institutional incentive structure shifted decisively. Banks and credit card issuers are now pulling deposits and tightening consumer credit ahead of May 29 consumer spending data. The risk is that credit withdrawal creates a self-fulfilling demand destruction loop—spending weakens, lenders' pessimism proves correct, and equities face capitulation selling on the realization that Warsh's rate cuts arrive into a weakening consumer and sticky oil, not a healing cycle.

active_themes.label: Lenders Front-Running Cuts
active_themes.summary: Credit withdrawal is now in motion, though no headline announcements arrived today. Banks and credit card issuers have zero ambiguity about Fed direction and clear incentive to tighten before the competitive race for lower-yield lending intensifies. Household debt sits at $18.8T all-time high. The May 29 consumer spending print will signal whether lenders' pessimism is prophetic or premature—and whether credit withdrawal creates self-fulfilling demand destruction.

active_themes.label: 30Y Yield at 2007 Highs
active_themes.summary: The 30-year yield closed at its highest level since June 2007. This reflects bond market conviction that Warsh cuts will weaken the dollar and push oil higher, forcing long-duration yields to reprice upward as inflation expectations reset. Equities are now pricing the same scenario: cuts into deteriorating trade-offs, not healing. The implication is no longer debated—it is institutional consensus.

open_watchlist.condition: Dollar index (DXY) closes below 100 for five consecutive trading days
open_watchlist.meaning: Signals market pricing of Warsh-era rate cuts and oil persistence simultaneously; typically precedes a 12-18 month period of dollar weakness and imported inflation.

open_watchlist.condition: Oil closes above $95 for three consecutive trading days (any cause: Iran escalation, inventory data, Warsh hawkish signal, or geopolitical escalation)
open_watchlist.meaning: Warsh's first rate-cut decision becomes a test of whether he is data-dependent (hold on oil risk) or politically driven (cut anyway); a break confirms structural inflation is the binding constraint.

open_watchlist.condition: Third major lender (Discover, Capital One, American Express) cuts deposit rates or tightens consumer credit within 7 days
open_watchlist.meaning: Confirms credit contraction is not a two-lender anomaly but a systemic dynamic; validates that institutions are front-running Fed rate cuts by restricting credit now.

open_watchlist.condition: April consumer spending (released May 29) shows MoM change of 0% or negative
open_watchlist.meaning: Lenders' credit withdrawal is prophetic; demand is already softening despite job gains in May; Warsh must choose between cutting into weakness (capitulation scenario) or pausing to protect the dollar.

open_watchlist.condition: Warsh's first public statement as Fed chair does not explicitly reference oil or supply constraints as a reason for gradualism
open_watchlist.meaning: Warsh is either ignoring the constraint or confident it will self-resolve; if he ignores it, bond markets will extract a yield premium immediately, forcing a sharp correction in equities within 1–2 weeks.

open_watchlist.condition: Oil closes below $88 and holds below that level for three consecutive trading days
open_watchlist.meaning: Demand destruction is real and severe; oil's geopolitical risk premium is collapsing; the deflationary signal is strong enough to let Warsh cut safely; bond yields will reprice lower; equities get a reprieve from capitulation selling.

open_watchlist.condition: A major lender (Discover, Capital One, or American Express) cuts deposit rates or tightens consumer credit within 7 days
open_watchlist.meaning: The institutional credit front-running is accelerating; the entire system expects demand destruction ahead; the pessimistic market narrative has become consensus; watch for immediate equity capitulation selling as the bear case shifts from tail risk to base case.

open_watchlist.condition: A second major lender (Discover, Capital One, or American Express) announces deposit rate cuts or consumer credit tightening within 7 days
open_watchlist.meaning: Credit withdrawal is in full swing and lenders are confident in demand destruction; paired with weak May 29 spending data, this triggers capitulation selling in equities.

open_watchlist.condition: April consumer spending (May 29 release) shows MoM change of 0% or negative
open_watchlist.meaning: Credit tightening is already working; demand is weakening into Warsh's confirmed rate cut cycle, setting up the scenario where cuts arrive too late and too weak to prevent recession.

open_watchlist.condition: Oil closes above $95 for three consecutive trading days (any cause: Iran escalation, inventory, or dollar weakness)
open_watchlist.meaning: The $90+ floor is breaking upward; inflation expectations are no longer stable and the long-duration repricing accelerates, forcing Warsh to signal hawkish gradualism or risk currency crisis.
